text: A guest book that knows who is coming. The lantern is lit.
picture: The Storyteller stands in a dark, misty hollow, holding a glowing red lantern low. Mist swirls around his boots. Far behind him, the faint, fog-shrouded glow of a roadside motel sign.

text: I work the night desk at the Wayside Motel, out on Route 9, where the road runs between two towns that don't talk to each other.
picture: June sits alone at the motel's front desk, lit by a single lamp, framed by the office window showing the dark, fog-shrouded night. She looks weary under the buzzing motel sign's glow. The empty road stretches past her.
sound: the faint buzz of the sign

text: Twelve rooms. Most nights, nobody comes.
picture: A nighttime view down the long, foggy motel walkway. All twelve doors are dark. Under a flickering security light, the only movement is fog creeping across the cracked concrete. The emptiness feels watchful and still.

text: The guest book sits open on the counter. The owner, Mr. Pell, likes ink. He says a name in ink is a promise.
picture: June, looking tired in her motel polo, leans over the counter, one finger tracing a line of dark blood-red ink in the open guest book. Grey dawn light spills through the office window.
sound: the quiet scratch of her finger on paper

text: Every morning, when I hand over the keys, there's a new line in it. Room six. Signed at two fourteen a. m. A different name every night.
picture: June stands at the dawn-lit front desk, holding the motel key ring. An open line in wet red ink in the guest book shows 'Room 6' and a new name. Her face shows quiet dread as she looks at it.

text: Room six has been boarded up since before I was hired.
picture: A weathered door, its brass number 6 hanging crooked. Thick, dusty planks nailed across it under a single yellow security light. Fog curls thickly around the base of the door and across the concrete walkway.
sound: the low hum of a distant highway

text: The first week, I blamed the day staff. The second week, I stopped blaming anyone. I started watching.
picture: June sits upright and alert at the front desk, phone in hand showing a dim security camera feed, the open guest book directly in front of her under the desk lamp's steady light.

text: Last night, at two thirteen, the lights in the parking lot flickered. At two fourteen, the pen moved.
picture: Extreme close-up on the fountain pen, slightly rolled away from its place on the open guest book, lit by the flickering glow of a dying desk lamp.

text: Not much. Just a roll. Like someone had brushed it with a sleeve.
picture: June's face, lit only by the ghostly blue light of her phone screen, eyes fixed on the display, refusing to look down at the counter.

text: I didn't look at the book. I looked at the camera. On the screen, I was sitting at the desk.
picture: Phone screen view: grainy security camera feed showing June at the desk from a high corner, a tall, slender silhouette in a dark raincoat standing close behind her.

text: And behind me, close enough to breathe on my neck, a
picture: Security camera angle: June sits frozen at the desk, the too-thin figure in the dripping dark raincoat now bending over her shoulder toward the guest book, its hooded face hidden.

text: man in a wet raincoat was leaning over my shoulder to write.
picture: Security camera angle: the hooded figure looms over June, one pale hand emerging from the raincoat sleeve, reaching toward the open guest book on the counter.

text: I didn't turn around. I couldn't.
picture: June seen from behind, still seated at the desk, her head held rigidly forward. The camera and the open guest book are in front of her. She is motionless, her back tense, as a single drop of water falls onto her shoulder.
sound: a single drop of water hitting the floor

text: When the lights came back, the office was empty.
picture: A wide shot of the empty motel office at night. Only the desk lamp is on, casting a sickly yellow pool on the guest book and counter. The rest of the room is in deep shadow, chairs and filing cabinets silhouetted. The effect is one of sudden, unsettling stillness.
sound: a low, persistent hum of empty electricity

text: The book was open. The ink was still wet. Room six. Two fourteen a. m. And the name was mine.
picture: A close-up of the open guest book on the motel counter. A fresh line in wet, glistening red ink reads 'June Marsh, Room 6'. Beside the book, a small, cold puddle of water reflects the desk lamp's light.
sound: the faint, slow drip of water from the counter's edge

text: Mr. Pell came in at six. He read the line very quietly.
picture: Mr. Pell stands at the motel counter, his thin frame in a brown cardigan. His expression is kind and profoundly sad as he stares down at the guest book, his reading glasses hanging unused on their cord. The morning light from a window behind him is pale and cold.

text: Then he took a key off the hook. A key I had never seen.
picture: A close-up of Mr. Pell's hand. His thin, age-spotted fingers hold an old, tarnished brass key on a red fob tag stamped with the number 6. It rests on the counter, distinct from the modern key hooks on the wall.
sound: the dull, heavy clink of the brass key on the wooden counter

text: "It's always the one at the desk," he said. "Your room's ready."
picture: Mr. Pell, his face weary and resigned, holds out the brass key towards June. June, out of focus in the extreme foreground, is a blurry silhouette of shock and fear, her green polo just visible. The morning light feels like a verdict.

text: The Wayside Motel is still open. The night desk is always staffed. And if you sign the book, check the name above yours.
picture: In the hollow, The Storyteller lowers his glowing red lantern, his face grave. Far behind him, the flickering neon motel sign 'Wayside' casts a sickly glow. One door at the far end of the row is boarded, yet stands slightly ajar, a dim, unnatural light spilling from within.
sound: a distant, faint buzz of neon
